Logic and sets

Source: vignettes/logic-and-sets.Rmd
logic-and-sets.Rmd

This vignette covers Boolean algebra (normal forms, minimization, and satisfiability) and sets: intervals, finite sets, the number sets, image sets, condition sets, ranges, set operations, and transfinite ordinals. The predicate based assumptions system (ask(), refine(), and assuming()) has its own vignette.

library(symcompR)
p <- Symbol("p"); q <- Symbol("q"); r <- Symbol("r")
w <- Symbol("w"); x <- Symbol("x"); y <- Symbol("y"); z <- Symbol("z")
n <- Symbol("n", integer = TRUE)

Boolean expressions

Symbols double as Boolean variables. And(), Or(), Not(), Xor(), Implies(), Equivalent(), and ITE() (if then else) build Boolean functions, and &, |, and ! work as operators.

And(p, Or(q, Not(p)))
#> p & (q | ~p)
(p & q) | !r
#> ~r | (p & q)
Implies(p, q)
#> Implies(p, q)
Equivalent(p, q)
#> Equivalent(p, q)
Xor(p, q)
#> p ^ q
And(p, TRUE)
#> p

Truth values are substituted with subs(), and truth_table() lists all assignments.

subs(And(p, q), list(list(p, S_true), list(q, S_false)))
#> False
truth_table(Implies(p, q))
#>       p     q value
#> 1 FALSE FALSE  TRUE
#> 2 FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
#> 3  TRUE FALSE FALSE
#> 4  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

Normal forms and simplification 

to_cnf(Or(And(p, q), r))
#> (p | r) & (q | r)
to_dnf(And(Or(p, q), r))
#> (p & r) | (q & r)
to_nnf(Not(Implies(p, q)))
#> p & ~q
eliminate_implications(Implies(p, q))
#> q | ~p
is_cnf(And(Or(p, q), r))
#> [1] TRUE
to_cnf(Equivalent(p, Or(q, r)), simplify = TRUE)
#> (p | ~q) & (p | ~r) & (q | r | ~p)

simplify_logic() finds a minimal equivalent expression with the Quine-McCluskey algorithm.

simplify_logic(Or(And(p, q), And(p, Not(q))))
#> p
simplify_logic((!p & !q & !r) | (!p & !q & r))
#> ~p & ~q
simplify_logic(Implies(p, q) & Implies(q, p), form = "cnf")
#> (p | ~q) & (q | ~p)

SOPform() and POSform() build a minimal sum of products or product of sums from the minterms of a truth table (the rows where the function is true), optionally with “don’t care” rows. Minterms are given as row numbers, so c(3, 7) over x, y, z means the rows 011 and 111.

SOPform(list(x, y, z), c(3, 7))
#> y & z
SOPform(list(x, y, z), c(1, 2, 5, 6))
#> (y & ~z) | (z & ~y)
POSform(list(w, x, y, z), c(1, 3, 7, 11, 15), dontcares = c(0, 2, 5))
#> z & (y | ~w)

Satisfiability

satisfiable() runs the DPLL algorithm. It returns a satisfying assignment, or FALSE when there is none. valid() tests whether an expression is a tautology.

satisfiable(And(p, Not(q)))
#> $p
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $q
#> [1] FALSE
satisfiable(And(p, Not(p)))
#> [1] FALSE
length(satisfiable(Or(p, q), all_models = TRUE))
#> [1] 3
valid(Or(p, Not(p)))
#> [1] TRUE

The remaining connectives are Nand(), Nor(), and the if then else function ITE(). is_dnf() and is_nnf() test for disjunctive and negation normal form.

Nand(TRUE, FALSE)
#> True
Nor(TRUE, FALSE)
#> False
Nand(x > 0, y > 0)
#> ~((x > 0) & (y > 0))
Nor(x > 0, y > 0)
#> ~((x > 0) | (y > 0))
ITE(TRUE, p, q)
#> p
c(is_dnf(Or(And(p, q), r)), is_dnf(And(p, Or(q, r))))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
c(is_nnf(And(Not(p), q)), is_nnf(Not(And(p, q))))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
distribute_or_over_and(And(Or(Not(p), q), r))
#> (q & r) | (r & ~p)

bool_map() decides whether two Boolean functions are the same up to a renaming of variables, and returns the renaming.

bool_map(Or(And(p, q), Not(p)), Or(And(x, y), Not(x)))
#> $expr
#> q | ~p
#> 
#> $mapping
#> $mapping$p
#> x
#> 
#> $mapping$q
#> y

Algebraic normal form and gates

The algebraic normal form (ANF) writes a Boolean function as an exclusive or of conjunctions. Xnor() is the negated exclusive or and Exclusive() says that at most one argument is true.

A <- Symbol("A"); B <- Symbol("B"); C <- Symbol("C")
Xnor(A, B)
#> ~(A ^ B)
Exclusive(A, B, C)
#> ~(A & B) & ~(A & C) & ~(B & C)
distribute_and_over_or(Or(And(A, B), C))
#> (A | C) & (B | C)
distribute_xor_over_and(And(A, Xor(B, C)))
#> (A & B) ^ (A & C)
to_anf(Or(x, y))
#> x ^ y ^ (x & y)
to_anf(Implies(x, y))
#> x ^ True ^ (x & y)
is_anf(Xor(x, And(x, y)))
#> [1] TRUE
is_anf(Or(x, y))
#> [1] FALSE
anf_coeffs(c(1, 1, 1, 0))
#> [1] 1 0 0 1
ANFform(list(x, y), c(1, 1, 1, 0))
#> True ^ (x & y)
bool_minterm(3, list(x, y))
#> x & y
bool_maxterm(3, list(x, y))
#> ~x | ~y
bool_monomial(3, list(x, y))
#> x & y
gateinputcount(Or(A, And(B, C)))
#> [1] 4

Inference

pl_true() evaluates a sentence in a partial model, entails() decides logical consequence and a PropKB() knowledge base answers queries about what it has been told. KB() is the base class.

literal_symbol(Not(A))
#> A
pl_true(Or(A, B), list(A = TRUE))
#> [1] TRUE
pl_true(And(A, B), list(A = TRUE))
#> [1] NA
entails(B, list(Implies(A, B), A))
#> [1] TRUE
entails(A, list(Or(A, B)))
#> [1] FALSE
kb <- PropKB()
kb$tell(Implies(A, B)); kb$tell(A)
kb$ask(B)
#> [1] TRUE
kb$ask(C)
#> [1] FALSE
kb$clauses()
#> [[1]]
#> A
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> B | ~A
kb$retract(A)
kb$ask(B)
#> [1] FALSE
KB()$clauses()
#> list()

The DPLL procedure decides satisfiability. Its steps work on clauses written with symbols, or with integers (to_int_repr()), where -i is the negation of the ith symbol.

dpll_satisfiable(And(A, Not(A)))
#> [1] FALSE
dpll(list(Or(A, B), Not(A)), list(A, B), list())
#> $A
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $B
#> [1] TRUE
find_pure_symbol(list(A, B), list(Or(A, Not(B)), Or(Not(B), A)))
#> [[1]]
#> A
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] TRUE
find_unit_clause(list(Or(A, B), A), list())
#> [[1]]
#> A
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] TRUE
unit_propagate(list(Or(A, B), Or(Not(A), B)), A)
#> [[1]]
#> B
to_int_repr(list(Or(x, y), Not(x)), list(x, y))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] -1
dpll_int_repr(list(c(1, 2), -1), c(1, 2), list())
#> $`1`
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $`2`
#> [1] TRUE
find_pure_symbol_int_repr(c(1, 2, 3), list(c(1, -2), c(-2, -3), c(3, 1)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] TRUE
find_unit_clause_int_repr(list(c(1, 2, 3), c(2, -3), c(1, -2)), list("1" = TRUE))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] FALSE
unit_propagate_int_repr(list(c(1, 2), c(3, -2), 2), 2)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 3
pl_true_int_repr(c(1, 2), list("1" = FALSE))
#> [1] NA
pl_true_int_repr(c(1, 2), list("1" = FALSE, "2" = FALSE))
#> [1] FALSE

dimacs_load() reads a formula in the DIMACS CNF format, and dimacs_load_file() reads it from a file:

dimacs_load("1 2 \n 3")
#> cnf_3 & (cnf_1 | cnf_2)
tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".cnf")
writeLines(c("1 -2 0", "3 0"), tf)
dimacs_load_file(tf)
#> cnf_3 & (cnf_1 | ~cnf_2)
unlink(tf)

Assumptions

The assumptions system, with ask() and refine(), has its own vignette, vignette("assumptions", package = "symcompR").

Sets

Intervals and finite sets

Interval(a, b) is closed by default; left_open and right_open change that, and Interval_open(), Interval_Lopen(), and Interval_Ropen() are shortcuts.

Interval(0, 1)
#> Interval(0, 1)
Interval(0, 1, TRUE, FALSE)
#> Interval.Lopen(0, 1)
Interval_open(0, 1)
#> Interval.open(0, 1)
Interval_Lopen(0, 1)
#> Interval.Lopen(0, 1)
Interval_Ropen(0, 1)
#> Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)
#> {1, 2, 3}

Set operations simplify their result whenever they can.

Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3), Interval(1, 2))
#> Interval(0, 3)
Union(Interval(0, 1), EmptySet)
#> Interval(0, 1)
Intersection(Interval(0, 1), UniversalSet)
#> Interval(0, 1)
PowerSet(FiniteSet(1, 2))
#> PowerSet({1, 2})
DisjointUnion(FiniteSet(1, 2), FiniteSet(3))
#> DisjointUnion({1, 2}, {3})
Intersection(Interval(0, 5), Interval(3, 10))
#> Interval(3, 5)
Complement(Interval(0, 5), Interval(1, 2))
#> Union(Interval.Ropen(0, 1), Interval.Lopen(2, 5))
Complement(Reals, FiniteSet(0))
#> Union(Interval.open(-oo, 0), Interval.open(0, oo))
SymmetricDifference(Interval(0, 3), Interval(2, 5))
#> Union(Interval.Ropen(0, 2), Interval.Lopen(3, 5))
Union(FiniteSet(1, 2, 3), FiniteSet(3, 4))
#> {1, 2, 3, 4}
Intersection(FiniteSet(1, 2, 3), Interval(2, 5))
#> {2, 3}
ProductSet(FiniteSet(1, 2), FiniteSet(3, 4))
#> ProductSet({1, 2}, {3, 4})

Membership, inclusion, and measure:

contains(Interval(0, 1), Rational(1, 2))
#> [1] TRUE
contains(Interval(0, 1), x)
#> (0 <= x) & (x <= 1)
is_subset(Interval(0, 1), Interval(-1, 2))
#> [1] TRUE
measure(Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 4)))
#> 3
boundary(Interval(0, 1, TRUE))
#> {0, 1}
set_inf(Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 4)))
#> 0
set_sup(Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 4)))
#> 4

contains() returns a condition when membership depends on a symbol, and as_relational() turns a set into the equivalent condition.

as_relational(Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3)), x)
#> ((0 <= x) & (x <= 1)) | ((2 <= x) & (x <= 3))

Number sets and ranges

Naturals, Naturals0, Integers, Rationals, Reals, and Complexes are the standard number sets. Range() is an arithmetic progression of integers, possibly infinite.

is_subset(Naturals, Integers)
#> [1] TRUE
Naturals0
#> Naturals0
Rationals
#> Rationals
Complexes
#> Complexes
contains(Rationals, Rational(1, 2))
#> [1] TRUE
Intersection(Integers, Interval(-2.5, 2))
#> Range(-2, 3, 1)
Range(1, 10, 3)
#> Range(1, 10, 3)
contains(Range(1, 10, 3), 7)
#> [1] TRUE
Intersection(Range(1, 10, 3), Interval(3, 8))
#> Range(4, 10, 3)
Range(0, oo, 2)
#> Range(0, oo, 2)

Image sets and condition sets

ImageSet(f, S) is the image \{f(s) : s \in S\}; imageset() simplifies it when possible. ConditionSet(x, cond, S) is \{x \in S : \text{cond}\}. These are the sets that solveset() returns for periodic and unsolved equations.

squares <- ImageSet(Lambda(x, x^2), Naturals)
squares
#> ImageSet(Lambda(x, x^2), Naturals)
contains(squares, 4)
#> [1] TRUE
imageset(Lambda(x, 2 * x), Integers)
#> ImageSet(Lambda(x, 2*x), Integers)
imageset(Lambda(x, x^2), Interval(-2, 1))
#> Interval(0, 4)
ConditionSet(x, Eq(sin(x), x), Interval(0, 1))
#> ConditionSet(x, Eq(sin(x), x), Interval(0, 1))

Complex regions

ComplexRegion() describes a region of the complex plane as a product of intervals, in rectangular or polar form.

R1 <- ComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 6)))
contains(R1, Rational(5, 2) + Rational(9, 2) * sym_I)
#> [1] TRUE
Intersection(ComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(1, 3), Interval(-1, 1))), Reals)
#> Interval(1, 3)
ComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval(0, 2 * sym_pi)), polar = TRUE)
#> PolarComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval.Ropen(0, 2*pi)))

a_interval(), b_interval(), and psets() return the parts of a region, complex_region_from_real() embeds a set of reals, and normalize_theta_set() reduces a set of angles to [0, 2\pi).

R2 <- ComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4)))
a_interval(R2)
#> Interval(1, 2)
b_interval(R2)
#> Interval(3, 4)
psets(R2)[[1]]
#> ProductSet(Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4))
complex_region_from_real(Interval(1, 2))
#> CartesianComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(1, 2), {0}))
normalize_theta_set(Interval(9 * sym_pi / 2, 5 * sym_pi))
#> Interval(pi/2, pi)
normalize_theta_set(Interval(-3 * sym_pi / 2, sym_pi / 2))
#> Interval.Ropen(0, 2*pi)

Set arithmetic

SetExpr() wraps a set so that arithmetic acts on all of its elements, which is interval arithmetic for intervals.

SetExpr(Interval(0, 1)) + 1
#> SetExpr(Interval(1, 2))
SetExpr(Interval(1, 2)) * SetExpr(Interval(10, 20))
#> SetExpr(Interval(10, 40))

Ordinals

symcompR implements ordinal numbers below \varepsilon_0 in Cantor normal form. ord_omega is \omega, and ordinal arithmetic is not commutative:

w <- ord_omega
w + 1
#> w + 1
1 + w
#> w
1 + w == w
#> [1] TRUE
(w + 3) * (w + 2)
#> w^2 + w*2 + 3
Ordinal(OmegaPower(3, 2), OmegaPower(1, 4), OmegaPower(0, 7))
#> w^3*2 + w*4 + 7
is_successor_ordinal(w^2 + 1)
#> [1] TRUE
is_limit_ordinal(w^2)
#> [1] TRUE
ord0
#> ord0
ord0 + 1
#> 1
ordinal_degree(w^2 + w * 3 + 1)
#> 2
